title: Timeouts and Long-Running Tasks knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Timeouts and Long-Running Tasks”?
options: Waiting for a specific child process
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Timeout strategies” under lesson 106, “Timeouts and Long-Running Tasks”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Timeouts and Long-Running Tasks”?
options: Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Bound concurrency, collect every child status, and clean up on interruption.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
questions.answer_key: Bound concurrency, collect every child status, and clean up on interruption.
questions.explanation: Bound concurrency, collect every child status, and clean up on interruption. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Timeouts and Long-Running Tasks”?
options: Track task lifecycles, define cleanup on normal exit and interruption, and collect each status.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
questions.answer_key: Track task lifecycles, define cleanup on normal exit and interruption, and collect each status.
questions.explanation: Track task lifecycles, define cleanup on normal exit and interruption, and collect each status. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
